title: Vil eller ha lyst til — expressing wants and preferences
goal: Choose vil for direct desire or intention and ha lyst til å/på for feeling inclined toward an activity or thing.

objectives.statement: Choose vil for direct desire or intention and ha lyst til å/på for feeling inclined toward an activity or thing.

spans.value: Emma and Jonas are staying with their friend Nora in Bergen. On Saturday morning, they are deciding what to do.
Hva vil dere gjøre i dag?

blocks.translation: What do you want to do today?

spans.value: Jeg vil se Bryggen først. Jeg har aldri vært der.

blocks.translation: I want to see Bryggen first. I’ve never been there.

spans.value: Greit. Etterpå har jeg lyst til å gå opp Fløyen.

blocks.translation: All right. Afterwards I feel like walking up Mount Fløyen.

spans.value: Gå opp? Jeg vil ta banen.

blocks.translation: Walk up? I want to take the railway.

spans.value: Vi kan bestemme det senere. Har dere lyst på frokost først?

blocks.translation: We can decide that later. Do you feel like having breakfast first?

spans.value: Ja, jeg har lyst på kaffe og noe varmt å spise.

blocks.translation: Yes, I feel like having coffee and something warm to eat.

spans.value: Jeg vil bare ha te. Og så vil jeg dra med en gang.

blocks.translation: I only want tea. And then I want to leave straight away.

spans.value: Da går vi til kafeen på hjørnet.

blocks.translation: Then we’ll go to the café on the corner.

spans.value: The three friends are all expressing wants, but they do not always use the same expression. Emma often states a clear choice or intention with
: she wants to see Bryggen, take the railway, and leave soon. Jonas describes what appeals to him at the moment with
: he feels like walking, and coffee sounds good to him.
That contrast is the focus of this chapter.

sections.title: A direct want or intention: vil

en.value: I want to see Bryggen.

en.value: I want to go home.

no.value: Jeg vil ha te.

sections.title: What appeals to you: ha lyst til å

spans.value: when an activity appeals to someone or when someone feels inclined to do it. English often uses

no.value: Jeg har lyst til å gå opp Fløyen.

en.value: I feel like walking up Mount Fløyen.

no.value: Nora har lyst til å spise ute.

en.value: Nora feels like eating out.

no.value: Vi har lyst til å besøke museet.

en.value: We feel like visiting the museum.

no.value: Har du lyst til å bli med?

en.value: Do you feel like coming along?

no.value: Jeg har lyst til å bade.

en.value: I feel like swimming.

no.value: Jeg har lyst til bade.

en.value: I feel like swimming.

spans.value: This form is incorrect because an activity after
changes in the usual way. In the present tense, it is

no.value: Jeg har lyst til å lage middag.

en.value: I feel like making dinner.

no.value: Hun har ikke lyst til å gå ut.

en.value: She doesn’t feel like going out.

spans.value: does not change according to the person:

no.value: Jeg har lyst til å danse.

en.value: I feel like dancing.

no.value: De har lyst til å danse.

en.value: They feel like dancing.

no.value: Etterpå har jeg lyst til å gå opp Fløyen.

en.value: Afterwards I feel like walking up Mount Fløyen.

spans.value: Walking appeals to him. His sentence sounds less like a fixed plan than Emma’s:

no.value: Jeg vil ta banen.

en.value: I want to take the railway.

spans.value: The difference is not that one wish is strong and the other weak in every situation. The important choice is how the speaker presents the wish:

items.value: presents a direct want or intention;
presents an activity as something the person feels inclined to do.

spans.value: The same activity can be expressed in two ways, depending on the intended meaning.

no.value: Jeg vil gå hjem nå.

en.value: I want to go home now.

no.value: Jeg har lyst til å gå en tur.

en.value: I feel like going for a walk.

spans.value: The first sentence states a direct wish or decision. The second describes an appealing activity.

no.value: Sara vil lage middag i kveld.

en.value: Sara wants to make dinner tonight.

no.value: Sara har lyst til å lage noe nytt.

en.value: Sara feels like making something new.

spans.value: In the first sentence, making dinner is Sara’s intended action. In the second, experimenting with something new appeals to her.

no.value: Vi vil besøke familien i helgen.

en.value: We want to visit the family this weekend.

no.value: Vi har lyst til å besøke den nye utstillingen.

en.value: We feel like visiting the new exhibition.

spans.value: A negative contrast is also useful:

no.value: Jeg vil ikke kjøre i kveld.

en.value: I don’t want to drive tonight.

no.value: Jeg har ikke lyst til å kjøre i regnet.

en.value: I don’t feel like driving in the rain.

spans.value: The first speaker directly rejects driving. The second describes a lack of inclination, connected here to the weather.

sections.title: Things that appeal to you: ha lyst på

spans.value: When the desired object is a thing, food, or drink, use

no.value: Jeg har lyst på kaffe.

en.value: I feel like having coffee.

no.value: Hun har lyst på is.

en.value: She feels like having ice cream.

no.value: Barna har lyst på pizza.

en.value: The children feel like having pizza.

no.value: Har dere lyst på frokost?

en.value: Do you feel like having breakfast?

no.value: Jeg har lyst til å spise.

en.value: I feel like eating.

no.value: Jeg har lyst på en sandwich.

en.value: I feel like having a sandwich.

no.value: Vi har lyst til å lage suppe.

en.value: We feel like making soup.

no.value: Vi har lyst på suppe.

en.value: We feel like having soup.

spans.value: This is the distinction Nora and Jonas use at the café:

no.value: Har dere lyst på frokost først?

en.value: Do you feel like having breakfast first?

no.value: Jeg har lyst på kaffe og noe varmt å spise.

en.value: I feel like having coffee and something warm to eat.

spans.value: Jonas is describing what sounds appealing to him at that moment.

no.value: Jeg vil ha en kaffe.

en.value: I want a coffee.

no.value: Jeg har lyst på kaffe.

en.value: I feel like having coffee.

spans.value: Both sentences can be natural. The first is a direct statement of what the speaker wants. The second emphasizes appetite, desire, or present inclination.

no.value: Mina vil ha den blå jakka.

en.value: Mina wants the blue jacket.

no.value: Mina har lyst på en ny jakke.

en.value: Mina feels like getting a new jacket.

spans.value: The first points to a direct choice: the blue jacket. The second describes the general appeal of getting a new jacket.

sections.title: Checkpoint: choose the correct lyst frame

spans.value: for things. Keep the situations connected to the café and the day in Bergen: ordering a drink, eating something warm, visiting a place, taking a walk, or buying a small souvenir.

no.value: Jeg vil besøke museet.

en.value: I want to visit the museum.

no.value: Jeg vil å besøke museet.

en.value: I want to visit the museum.

no.value: Hun har lyst til å reise.

en.value: She feels like travelling.

no.value: Hun har lyst til reise.

en.value: She feels like travelling.

no.value: De har lyst til å svømme.

en.value: They feel like swimming.

no.value: De har lyst på å svømme.

en.value: They feel like swimming.

spans.value: before a noun, not before an infinitive activity.
Using til å before a thing

no.value: Jeg har lyst på sjokolade.

en.value: I feel like having chocolate.

no.value: Jeg har lyst til å sjokolade.

en.value: I feel like having chocolate.

spans.value: Treating vil and har lyst til å as mechanically interchangeable

no.value: Oskar vil flytte til Trondheim.

en.value: Oskar wants to move to Trondheim.

spans.value: This presents moving as his direct desire or intention.

no.value: Oskar har lyst til å besøke Trondheim.

en.value: Oskar feels like visiting Trondheim.

spans.value: This presents a visit as something appealing. Replacing one form with the other changes how the wish is framed, even when both sentences remain grammatical.
After breakfast, the weather changes. The friends reconsider their plan.
Nå regner det ganske mye. Vil dere fortsatt dra til Fløyen?

blocks.translation: It’s raining quite a lot now. Do you still want to go to Fløyen?

spans.value: Nei, jeg har ikke lyst til å gå opp i dette været.

blocks.translation: No, I don’t feel like walking up in this weather.

spans.value: Jeg vil fortsatt ta banen, men jeg har også lyst til å se et museum.

blocks.translation: I still want to take the railway, but I also feel like seeing a museum.

spans.value: Hva har du mest lyst til?

blocks.translation: What do you feel most like doing?

spans.value: Jeg tror jeg har mest lyst til å gå på museum.

blocks.translation: I think I feel most like going to a museum.

spans.value: Enig. Og etterpå har jeg lyst på noe søtt.

blocks.translation: Agreed. And afterwards I feel like having something sweet.

spans.value: Da vil jeg vise dere en kafé jeg liker.

blocks.translation: Then I want to show you a café I like.

spans.value: The new dialogue reuses all three patterns:

no.value: Vil dere fortsatt dra til Fløyen?

en.value: Do you still want to go to Fløyen?

spans.value: This asks whether the original intention remains.

no.value: Jeg har ikke lyst til å gå opp i dette været.

en.value: I don’t feel like walking up in this weather.

spans.value: Jonas no longer feels inclined to do the activity.

no.value: Jeg har lyst på noe søtt.

en.value: I feel like having something sweet.

spans.value: The desired item is a thing, so Jonas uses
Emma uses both expressions in one turn:

no.value: Jeg vil fortsatt ta banen, men jeg har også lyst til å se et museum.

en.value: I still want to take the railway, but I also feel like seeing a museum.

spans.value: Her first idea remains a direct want. Her second idea is another activity that now appeals to her. This shows why the two expressions are useful together: they let a speaker distinguish a chosen intention from a present inclination.
